clips.title: Talk: Harry Percival - Stop Using Mocks (for a while)
clips.why: Harry Percival, author of a well-known Python testing book, shows on real code why tests built on mocks become fragile and hard to read.
look: How the mocks tie the test to the exact calls the code makes.
What happens to those tests when the code is changed but still works.
Why the test no longer tells you whether the program does the right thing.
clips.after: This is the story of the scans bucket: the mock test was green for broken code and red for the fix.

clips.title: Talk: Harry Percival - Stop Using Mocks (for a while)
clips.why: Later in the same talk he builds a fake for the same code, the move this lesson makes with the object store.
look: The fake implements the same small interface as the real adapter.
It keeps its state in plain Python data structures.
The tests now check results, not which methods were called.
clips.after: fcp's planned object-store fake is the same shape: the interface StorageService already uses, a dictionary inside, and a contract suite against MinIO.

practice.q: Which test checks an outcome rather than a call?

options.why: This checks how the code talks to storage. A correct refactor that changes the call turns it red.

options.text: assert import_scan(store, "wg-1", "b.csv", b"x") == 2 with an in-memory fake
options.why: It checks what the user would see: after two imports there are two files. Any correct implementation passes it.
Counting calls is still about how the code works, not about the result.

practice.q: Make this fixture run every test that uses it once on the fake and once on MinIO.
practice.hint: The same idea as parametrize, but on a fixture.
practice.why: A fixture with params runs once per value, and request.param tells it which target to build, so each test appears as [memory] and [minio].

practice.q: Your fake store quietly creates a bucket when you write into one that does not exist. Real S3 raises NoSuchBucket. Why is the friendly fake dangerous?

options.text: It is slower than the strict version.
options.why: Speed is not the issue. Behaviour is.

options.text: Tests using it pass for code that fails in production, which is exactly the mock's problem again.
options.why: A fake is only useful if it fails where the real service fails. Be loud about errors.

options.text: It uses more memory, because it keeps empty buckets.
options.why: A few empty dictionaries cost nothing. Hiding a production failure costs a lot.

practice.q: MinIO starts rejecting something your fake accepts. Put the steps in order.
items: Write a contract test that does exactly that thing
Run the suite with the real service: it passes on [minio] and fails on [memory]
Change the fake until the test passes on [memory] too
Every test that uses the fake now gets the real behaviour
practice.why: The real service is the reference. The contract test captures its behaviour, and fixing the fake once fixes it for every test that depends on it.

practice.q: The production module imports.py builds its client in get_store(). Swap in the fake at that seam for one test.
practice.hint: The monkeypatch method that replaces a name inside a module.
practice.why: monkeypatch.setattr replaces get_store in the module that calls it, and undoes the change when the test ends.
